newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget talks seen entering new phase.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget talks seen entering new phase.

text.p: The White House and Congress reopened stalled budget negotiations Tuesday with Republican leaders vowing to go ahead with their own plan if compromises on spending and taxes are not reached soon.

President Clinton urged his negotiators to remain flexible as discussions get under way on the numerous thorny issues that must be resolved before they can shake hands on a deal to balance the budget by 2002.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, stressed the importance of progress in this week's talks, which were to open with discussion of plans to rein in growth in the Medicare health care programme.

"I perceive that we enter a new phase today, this afternoon. We will continue this discussion with high-level representatives of the president through this week," he said, adding he was ready to give it "four to five solid days."
If no deal is reached Domenici and his House counterpart said they were ready to work with moderate Democrats to produce a budget with a tax cut.
Disputes between the White House and the Republicans in the last Congress led to Clinton's veto of spending bills and two partial government shutdowns.

"We hope we can reach an agreement with the president. If we can't we will have a strong proposal ourselves. We have been working on this for a long time," House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, told reporters.

The bargaining opened at 1 p.m. EDT in a room tucked away in the basement of the Capitol with a discussion of ways to control the growth of spending on Medicare, the programme that serves 63 million elderly and disabled persons.
Clinton was to send as his representatives Office of Management and Budget Director Franklin Raines, congressional liaison John Hilley and National Economic Council Chairman Gene Sperling.

Earlier in the day, Raines said he hoped the talks would lead to the "culmination" of the current budget process and the administration would find $100 billion in savings from Medicare over the next five years.

Republican leaders emerged from a closed-door session in House Speaker Newt Gingrich's office with statements that they remained committed to substantial tax cuts for families and investors. Their position was thrown into confusion before Congress recessed last month when the Georgia Republican angered conservative colleagues by suggesting the possibility of voting on a tax cut after a balanced budget deal.

Earlier in the day, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said administration officials had orders from the president to be "flexible" in the talks. Asked what he meant, McCurry told reporters: "I think that we understand that we're going to have show some flexibility if we want to achieve a balanced budget agreement. The president wants to work with this Republican Congress to achieve a balanced budget agreement."
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi has repeatedly criticised the White House for refusing to move off the budget plan it outlined in February.
